name: Paradys
description: A star 137 parsecs away, 56 times the Sun's width, measured from its light.

radius.source: McDonald, Zijlstra & Watson (2017), MNRAS 471, 770, table 2, HIP 72370: radius 55.698 solar radii, implied by the fitted luminosity 868.958 solar luminosities (fractional uncertainty 0.062) and temperature

temperature.source: McDonald, Zijlstra & Watson (2017), MNRAS 471, 770, table 2, HIP 72370: effective temperature 4202 +/- 125 K, from the fit of a model atmosphere to the star's spectral energy distribution (goodness of fit Q 0.043)

distance.source: McDonald, Zijlstra & Watson (2017), MNRAS 471, 770, table 2, HIP 72370: distance 136.986 pc, the paper's parallax inverted (Gaia DR1's where it revised the star's, else the Hipparcos reduction of van Leeuwen 2007; section 2.3; fractional uncertainty 0.018), at which the luminosity and radius hold

limb.none: no mass is measured and no spectroscopic surface gravity is published with this radius: McDonald, Zijlstra & Watson (2017), MNRAS 471, 770 assume the gravity of their fit (table column 15)

text.card: A star 137 parsecs away, 56 times the Sun's width, measured from its light.
text.introduction: Its brightness, measured band by band, gives 869 times the Sun's luminosity at 4,202 K, so 55.698 solar radii.
text.locator: Table 2, HIP 72370: D, Teff, L, Rad, Q

quotes.title: Alpha Apodis
quotes.card: Alpha Apodis, also named Paradys, is the brightest star in the southern circumpolar constellation of Apus.
quotes.introduction: It had the Greek alpha designation as part of the constellation which Johann Bayer called Apis Indica in his 1603 Uranometria star atlas.

radialVelocity.source: SIMBAD's radial velocity for Gaia DR3 5773473920382493440 (quality A), from 2006AstL...32..759G; Gaia DR3 measures none
